title: Dedekind Domains and the Failure of Unique Element Factorization in ℤ[√-5]
description: Proves that Dedekind domains generalize unique factorization from elements to ideals, while demonstrating that element-level factorization can fail. The classic example ℤ[√-5] is a Dedekind domain where 6 = 2·3 = (1+√-5)(1-√-5) gives two distinct irreducible factorizations. The element 2 is proved irreducible (norm analysis: N = 2 or 3 are impossible) but not prime (N(2) = 4 does not divide N(1±√-5) = 6), so ℤ[√-5] is not a UFD despite being a Dedekind domain. Proves: PID → Dedekind, prime ideals = maximal ideals in Dedekind domains, norm multiplicativity, and the unit characterization N = 1.

sections.title: Imports and Setup
sections.summary: Imports Mathlib and the parent Bezout/UFD chain file. Module header describes Dedekind domains, ideal unique factorization, and the ℤ[√-5] counterexample. Defines the ZSqrtNeg5 abbreviation for ℤ[√-5] = Zsqrtd(-5).
sections.mathContext: Dedekind domains satisfy: every nonzero prime ideal is maximal (Krull dimension ≤ 1). The ideal FTA states every nonzero proper ideal factors uniquely into prime ideals — the right generalization of the FTA from elements to ideals.

sections.title: Dedekind Domain Instances
sections.summary: Establishes that ℤ and k[x] (polynomial ring over a field) are Dedekind domains via inference. Proves pid_is_dedekind: every PID is a Dedekind domain. Proves prime_ideal_is_maximal via IsDedekindDomain.dimensionLtOne.
sections.mathContext: The hierarchy EuclideanDomain → PID → Dedekind domain → IntegralDomain holds. The characterization of Dedekind domains by Krull dimension forces every nonzero prime ideal to be maximal.

sections.title: Norm Theory for ℤ[√-5]
sections.summary: Proves norm_formula (N(a+b√-5) = a²+5b²), norm_nonneg, norm_mul_eq (multiplicativity), and norm computations for the four factors: N(2)=4, N(3)=9, N(1±√-5)=6. Private lemmas show N=2 and N=3 have no solutions by bounding b and using interval_cases on re.
sections.mathContext: The norm N: ℤ[√d] → ℤ sends a+b√d ↦ a²-db². For d=-5 this gives N = a²+5b² ≥ 0. Multiplicativity N(αβ) = N(α)N(β) is the key tool for factorization proofs. Elements with N=1 are exactly the units.

sections.title: Unit Characterization
sections.summary: Proves isUnit_iff_norm_one: z is a unit in ℤ[√-5] iff N(z) = 1. Forward direction: N(z)·N(z⁻¹) = 1 with nonnegativity forces N(z) = 1. Backward direction: if N(z) = 1, then z·conj(z) = ⟨N(z),0⟩ = 1 exhibits an explicit inverse. Proves two_not_unit from N(2) = 4 ≠ 1.
sections.mathContext: Units of ℤ[√d] with d < 0 have norm 1; for d = -5, the only units are ±1 (N = 1 forces a = ±1, b = 0 from a²+5b² = 1). The conjugate z* = a-b√-5 gives the inverse when N(z) = 1.

sections.title: Irreducibility vs. Primality of 2
sections.summary: Proves two_irreducible: if 2 = a·b then N(a)·N(b) = 4, and since N=2 and N=3 are impossible, exactly one of N(a)=1 or N(b)=1. Proves two_not_prime: 2 | (1+√-5)(1-√-5) = 6 but 2 ∤ (1±√-5) because N(2)=4 ∤ N(1±√-5)=6, giving a norm divisibility contradiction.
sections.mathContext: Irreducible means non-unit with no non-trivial factorization. Prime means: p|ab implies p|a or p|b. In a UFD these coincide; in ℤ[√-5] they diverge: 2 is irreducible (norm forces factor to be a unit) but not prime (fails to divide either factor of its product).

sections.title: Non-UFD Conclusion and Structural Results
sections.summary: Proves zsqrtneg5_not_ufd: in a UFD irreducible implies prime (UniqueFactorizationMonoid.irreducible_iff_prime), so two_irreducible + two_not_prime contradicts UFD status. Proves irred_imp_prime_in_ufd, hierarchy (PID → Dedekind ∧ UFD), and zsqrtneg5_witness bundling all three facts.
sections.mathContext: The theorem that UFDs have irreducible = prime is Mathlib's UniqueFactorizationMonoid.irreducible_iff_prime. The key implication: Dedekind domain is a UFD iff it is a PID. Since ℤ[√-5] is not a UFD, it is not a PID — its ideal class group has order 2, generated by the ideal (2, 1+√-5).

overview.historicalContext: Richard Dedekind introduced Dedekind domains in 1871 while studying algebraic integers and developing ideal theory. His key insight was that while element-level unique factorization fails in rings like ℤ[√-5], it is restored at the level of ideals. The example ℤ[√-5] with its dual factorization 6 = 2·3 = (1+√-5)(1-√-5) — recognized by Kummer and Dedekind — was the historical impetus for ideal theory. Ernst Kummer had earlier introduced 'ideal numbers' to restore unique factorization, and Dedekind reformulated this rigorously as ideals in 1871. This formalization proves the essential classical facts: 2 is irreducible but not prime, ℤ[√-5] fails to be a UFD, and Dedekind domains are exactly the right setting where ideal unique factorization holds.
overview.problemStatement: Let $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ denote the ring of algebraic integers $\{a+b\sqrt{-5} : a, b \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ with norm $N(a+b\sqrt{-5}) = a^2+5b^2$. The dual factorization $6 = 2 \cdot 3 = (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ shows element-level unique factorization fails. Prove: (1) 2 is irreducible (any factorization $2 = ab$ has $N(a) \in \{1,4\}$, so $a$ or $b$ is a unit); (2) 2 is not prime ($2 \mid (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ but $4 \nmid 6$); (3) $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ is not a UFD.
overview.proofStrategy: The proof has four phases: (1) Dedekind instances — establish ℤ and k[x] as Dedekind domains by typeclass inference, and prove prime_ideal_is_maximal via IsDedekindDomain.dimensionLtOne. (2) Norm theory — prove N(a+b√-5)=a²+5b²  is multiplicative and compute N for the four factors of 6. (3) Norm gap — prove a²+5b²≠2 and ≠3 by bounding b=0 with nlinarith and exhausting a∈{-1,0,1} with interval_cases. (4) Divergence — from the norm gap, any factorization 2=ab has N(a)∈{1,4}, proving irreducibility; the equation 6=4·N(k) has no solution, proving non-primality; UniqueFactorizationMonoid.irreducible_iff_prime then gives a contradiction with UFD.
keyInsights: The norm gap — a²+5b² ≠ 2 and ≠ 3 for any integers a, b — is the arithmetic heart of the proof. This gap exists because 2 is not a quadratic residue mod 5, making the prime 2 ramify as (2,1+√-5)² rather than split in ℤ[√-5].

The norm divisibility criterion converts element divisibility questions into integer arithmetic: α ∤ β iff N(α) ∤ N(β). Since N(2)=4 and N(1±√-5)=6, and 4 ∤ 6, we get 2 ∤ (1±√-5) — no Lean divisibility search needed.

Mathlib's UniqueFactorizationMonoid.irreducible_iff_prime is the bridge between the element-level properties and the UFD conclusion: it converts the two properties (irreducible, not prime) into a direct contradiction with any UFD instance.

The Lean proof uses decide for the dual factorization 2·3 = (1+√-5)(1-√-5) and norm computations, reducing concrete arithmetic in ℤ[√-5] to kernel computation. This demonstrates the power of decidability in formal mathematics.

The ideal class group Cl(ℤ[√-5]) ≅ ℤ/2ℤ is the algebraic invariant behind this failure: the non-principal ideal (2,1+√-5) has class of order 2, and the two element factorizations of 6 correspond to the two ways of decomposing the principal ideal (6) = p₁²·p₂·p₃ into prime ideal products.
prerequisites: Commutative ring theory: definition of integral domain, ideal, prime ideal, maximal ideal
Dedekind domain axiomatization: Noetherian, integrally closed in field of fractions, Krull dimension ≤ 1 (Mathlib.RingTheory.DedekindDomain.Basic)
Zsqrtd construction: the ring ℤ[√d] = {a + b√d : a, b ∈ ℤ} with multiplication (a+b√d)(c+e√d) = (ac+dbe) + (ae+bc)√d (Mathlib.NumberTheory.Zsqrtd.Basic)
Norm map on ℤ[√d]: N(a+b√d) = a² − d·b², multiplicative, and N(z) = 1 ↔ z is a unit
UniqueFactorizationMonoid typeclass: in any UFD, irreducible ↔ prime (Mathlib.RingTheory.UniqueFactorizationDomain)
Irreducible vs Prime in a commutative monoid with zero: definitions and the basic implication prime ⇒ irreducible (which holds in any integral domain)
Mathlib tactics decide, native_decide for finite computations in ℤ[√-5]; interval_cases for exhausting bounded integers; nlinarith for nonlinear arithmetic over ℝ/ℤ
IsDedekindDomain.dimensionLtOne: in a Dedekind domain, every nonzero prime ideal is maximal — the geometric statement of Krull dimension ≤ 1
Star structure on ℤ[√d]: conjugate (a+b√d)* = a − b√d, used to construct multiplicative inverses for unit elements via z·z* = N(z)

conclusion.summary: The file proves 24 theorems with 0 sorries and 0 axioms, fully machine-checked. Key results: 2 is irreducible in ℤ[√-5] (norm analysis closes all factorization cases); 2 is not prime (norm divisibility 4 ∤ 6 gives contradiction); ℤ[√-5] is not a UFD (irreducible ≠ prime via UniqueFactorizationMonoid.irreducible_iff_prime); PID → Dedekind domain (inferInstance); prime ideals = maximal ideals in Dedekind domains (IsDedekindDomain.dimensionLtOne).
conclusion.implications: This proof places ℤ[√-5] within the broader landscape of algebraic number theory: it is a Dedekind domain with class number 2, the simplest example of a ring of algebraic integers that fails unique factorization. Dedekind's resolution — ideal unique factorization — is now the foundation of algebraic number theory, class field theory, and arithmetic geometry. The ideal class group Cl(K) for a number field K measures the 'distance' from unique element factorization; this proof formalizes the simplest non-trivial example. The machinery of Zsqrtd norms and the interval_cases strategy used here generalizes to other quadratic rings ℤ[√d], enabling systematic Lean verification of class number computations.
openQuestions: Can the ideal class group of ℤ[√-5] be proved to have order exactly 2 in Lean 4, formalizing the complete obstruction? Proving Cl(ℤ[√-5]) ≅ ℤ/2ℤ would require showing (2,1+√-5)² = (2) (principal) while (2,1+√-5) itself is not principal.

Can Mathlib's ideal FTA be applied concretely to ℤ[√-5] to write out the prime ideal factorization (6) = (2,1+√-5)²·(3,1+√-5)·(3,1-√-5), making the connection between element and ideal factorizations computationally tangible?

For which values of d does ℤ[√d] have class number 1 (i.e., is a UFD/PID), and can Lean verify these computationally? The Stark-Heegner theorem says there are exactly 9 such negative d: -1,-2,-3,-7,-11,-19,-43,-67,-163.

mainTheorems.name: zsqrtneg5_not_ufd
mainTheorems.significance: **The headline theorem.** ℤ[√-5] is the canonical example of a Dedekind domain that fails element-level unique factorization. Proof: in a UFD, `UniqueFactorizationMonoid.irreducible_iff_prime` forces irreducible ⇔ prime; but `two_irreducible` and `two_not_prime` give an explicit witness of irreducible-but-not-prime. The contradiction is fully constructive.
mainTheorems.description: ℤ[√-5] is NOT a unique factorization monoid. Combines two_irreducible and two_not_prime via Mathlib's UniqueFactorizationMonoid.irreducible_iff_prime.

mainTheorems.name: two_irreducible
mainTheorems.significance: First half of the non-UFD witness. If $2 = ab$ then $N(a) \cdot N(b) = N(2) = 4$; the norm gap (no element has $N = 2$ or $N = 3$) forces $\{N(a), N(b)\} = \{1, 4\}$, hence one factor is a unit. Discharged by interval_cases on $a^2 + 5b^2 \in \{1,2,3,4\}$.
mainTheorems.description: 2 is irreducible in ℤ[√-5]: norm divisibility analysis closes every nontrivial factorization.

mainTheorems.name: two_not_prime
mainTheorems.significance: Second half of the non-UFD witness. $2 \mid (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5}) = 6$ by construction, but if $2 \mid (1 \pm \sqrt{-5}) = 2k$ then $6 = N(1 \pm \sqrt{-5}) = N(2) \cdot N(k) = 4 \cdot N(k)$, forcing $4 \mid 6$ — impossible by `omega`.
mainTheorems.description: 2 is not prime in ℤ[√-5]: norm divisibility 4 ∤ 6 blocks the prime-divides-one-factor implication.

mainTheorems.name: isUnit_iff_norm_one
mainTheorems.significance: The Norm-Unit Bridge — converts the abstract unit predicate into a finite arithmetic condition. Forward direction: $N(z) \cdot N(z^{-1}) = N(1) = 1$ with $N \geq 0$ forces $N(z) = 1$. Backward direction: $z \cdot z^* = \langle N(z), 0 \rangle = 1$ when $N(z) = 1$, exhibiting $z^*$ as inverse. Used by `two_irreducible` to convert $N(a) = 1$ into IsUnit a.
mainTheorems.description: A Zsqrtd element is a unit iff its norm equals 1. Discharged using the star/conjugate to build the inverse.

mainTheorems.name: norm_mul_eq
mainTheorems.statement: $\forall a, b : \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}],\ N(a \cdot b) = N(a) \cdot N(b)$
mainTheorems.significance: Multiplicativity of the norm — the workhorse identity. Reduces multiplicative questions in ℤ[√-5] to multiplicative questions about integer norms, where divisibility is decidable. Proved by unfolding Zsqrtd.norm and Zsqrtd.mul_def, then `ring`.
mainTheorems.description: The norm N(a+b√-5) = a²+5b² is multiplicative. Critical for both two_irreducible (norm product = 4) and two_not_prime (norm product = 6 with factor 4).

mainTheorems.name: prime_ideal_is_maximal
mainTheorems.statement: $\forall R\ [\mathrm{IsDedekindDomain}\ R]\ (p : \mathrm{Ideal}\ R),\ p \neq \bot \to p.\mathrm{IsPrime} \to p.\mathrm{IsMaximal}$
mainTheorems.significance: The Krull-dimension-≤-1 condition that distinguishes Dedekind domains from general Noetherian integrally closed rings. Used to motivate the ideal-level FTA: in a Dedekind domain, every nonzero proper ideal factors uniquely into a product of maximal (= prime) ideals.
mainTheorems.description: In a Dedekind domain, every nonzero prime ideal is maximal. Direct application of IsDedekindDomain.dimensionLtOne.

mainTheorems.name: pid_is_dedekind
mainTheorems.significance: Establishes the inclusion PID ⊂ Dedekind via Mathlib's instance chain. Discharged by `inferInstance`. The converse fails in general (Dedekind ≠ PID): ℤ[√-5] is Dedekind but not PID (class number 2).
mainTheorems.description: Every PID is a Dedekind domain. Establishes the standard hierarchy EuclideanDomain ⊂ PID ⊂ Dedekind.

mainTheorems.name: irred_imp_prime_in_ufd
mainTheorems.statement: $\forall R\ [\mathrm{CancelCommMonoidWithZero}\ R]\ [\mathrm{UniqueFactorizationMonoid}\ R]\ (p : R),\ \mathrm{Irreducible}\ p \to \mathrm{Prime}\ p$
mainTheorems.significance: The contrapositive used by `zsqrtneg5_not_ufd`: in any UFD, irreducible elements must be prime. ℤ[√-5] violates this implication via the explicit witness 2.
mainTheorems.description: In a UFD, irreducible implies prime. Wraps UniqueFactorizationMonoid.irreducible_iff_prime.mp.

mainTheorems.name: hierarchy
mainTheorems.statement: $\forall R\ [\mathrm{CommRing}\ R]\ [\mathrm{IsDomain}\ R]\ [\mathrm{IsPrincipalIdealRing}\ R],\ \mathrm{IsDedekindDomain}\ R \wedge \mathrm{UniqueFactorizationMonoid}\ R$
mainTheorems.significance: Bundles the two PID-derivable typeclasses. In the Dedekind setting, Dedekind+UFD ⇔ PID, so this conjunction characterizes PIDs among Dedekind domains.
mainTheorems.description: Every PID is both a Dedekind domain and a UFD. The Dedekind+UFD ⇒ PID converse is true in this setting (proved separately in Mathlib).

mainTheorems.name: zsqrtneg5_witness
mainTheorems.significance: The packaged non-UFD certificate. Combines the irreducibility of 2, its non-primality, and the explicit dual factorization $6 = 2 \cdot 3 = (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ into a single shareable record for downstream consumers.
mainTheorems.description: Summary witness bundling all three facts that establish ℤ[√-5] as a non-UFD.

crossReferences.description: Direct parent (FTA Generalization to Euclidean Domains): established that every Euclidean domain is a UFD via the chain EuclideanDomain → GCDMonoid → UniqueFactorizationMonoid. The open question raised there — whether unique factorization generalizes to the broader Dedekind setting — is answered HERE: it does, but only at the level of ideals, with ℤ[√-5] as the explicit witness that element-level factorization can fail.

Sibling (Gaussian Integers: Euclidean Domain and Prime Classification): ℤ[i] is the well-behaved counterpoint to ℤ[√-5]. Both are quadratic rings with a norm, but ℤ[i] is Euclidean (hence PID, UFD, Dedekind — all four typeclasses) while ℤ[√-5] sits one rung lower (Dedekind only). The norm-based factorization technique used in both files is the same; only the arithmetic of the norm differs (a²+b² for ℤ[i] vs a²+5b² for ℤ[√-5]).

Sibling (ℤ[√-2] as a Euclidean Domain): another quadratic ring of integers where ℤ[√d] IS a Euclidean domain. ℤ[√-2] (class number 1) and ℤ[√-5] (class number 2) bracket the Stark-Heegner classification — the 9 negative d for which ℤ[√d] is a UFD are d ∈ {-1,-2,-3,-7,-11,-19,-43,-67,-163}, and this file's non-UFD ℤ[√-5] is the smallest |d| for which it fails.

Sibling (Fermat's Two-Square Theorem via Gaussian Integers): an application of the ℤ[i] machinery from the parent sibling. The two-square theorem (p sum of two squares iff p = 2 or p ≡ 1 mod 4) and the failure of unique factorization in ℤ[√-5] (this entry) together illustrate how the class number of a quadratic ring controls which classical number-theoretic results lift to that ring.

Grandparent (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic from Euclid's Lemma): proves the FTA for ℤ via Euclid's lemma. The chain ℤ → Euclidean domain → PID → Dedekind ⊂ {ℤ[√-5]} extends this classical result to algebraic number rings; the present entry is the natural limit, showing where the element-level FTA breaks down.

Great-grandparent (Bézout's Identity): the root of this research lineage. Bézout → Euclid → FTA → FTA-for-Euclidean-domains → Dedekind-domain-FTA (ideal-level). This file completes the lineage by exhibiting the obstacle that motivated the shift from elements to ideals in the first place.

Direct precursor (Euclid's Lemma via coprime_iff_linear_combination): Euclid's lemma is the engine behind the standard FTA proof; the failure of unique factorization in ℤ[√-5] can be diagnosed as the failure of Euclid's lemma at the element level (2 divides a product without dividing either factor), restored only at the ideal level.

references.title: Über die Theorie der ganzen algebraischen Zahlen
references.venue: Supplement X to Dirichlet's *Vorlesungen über Zahlentheorie* (2nd edition), Vieweg, Braunschweig
references.note: The foundational treatise introducing ideals as the right algebraic objects to restore unique factorization. Dedekind's resolution of Kummer's 'ideal numbers' as actual sub-modules of an algebraic number ring is the conceptual leap that this file's main theorem (Dedekind ⊊ UFD) makes precise.

references.title: Zur Theorie der complexen Zahlen
references.venue: Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik (Crelle's Journal), Vol. 35, pp. 319–326
references.note: Introduces 'ideal numbers' (Idealzahlen) to restore unique factorization in cyclotomic rings ℤ[ζₚ] where it fails for p ≥ 23. The historical motivation for Dedekind's ideals; ℤ[√-5] is the simplest non-cyclotomic example of the same phenomenon.

references.title: Number Fields
references.note: Standard introductory text on algebraic number theory. Chapter 3 (Dedekind domains) gives the textbook treatment of ideal unique factorization, including the ℤ[√-5] example and the class group computation Cl(ℤ[√-5]) ≅ ℤ/2ℤ formalized in spirit by this file.

references.title: Algebraic Number Theory (2nd edition)
references.note: Reference treatment of Dedekind domains and class field theory. The hierarchy EuclideanDomain → PID → Dedekind formalized in this entry's `pid_is_dedekind` and `hierarchy` theorems appears in Chapter I, §3–4.

references.title: A complete determination of the complex quadratic fields of class-number one
references.note: Completes Heegner's 1952 proof of the Stark-Heegner theorem: ℤ[√d] (d < 0 squarefree) is a UFD iff d ∈ {-1,-2,-3,-7,-11,-19,-43,-67,-163}. The present entry's ℤ[√-5] is the smallest |d| ≡ 3 mod 4 not on this list and is therefore the natural minimal non-UFD example.

references.title: Algebraic Geometry
references.note: Chapter I, §6 introduces the geometric picture: a Dedekind domain is precisely the coordinate ring of a regular irreducible affine curve. The Krull-dimension-≤-1 condition encoded in `IsDedekindDomain.dimensionLtOne` corresponds to the curve being 1-dimensional.
